title: Resolve support tickets faster with full customer context
description: How Strawberry rebuilds a ticket's story across billing, product data, docs, and team chat, then drafts the reply or hands engineering a case it can act on.

navigation.title: Customer Support & Success
navigation.tagline: Resolve tickets faster with every source in view

introduction: A customer writes in: I bought credits, they never arrived, and now I can't use the product. That is the whole ticket. Before anyone can reply, someone has to open the payment processor, the credit ledger, the account's live balance, and the app logs, and hope the timestamps agree with each other.

Strawberry is a browser with AI companions that work across the tabs and apps your team is already signed into. For support, that means a companion can do that checking before you open the ticket, put the events in order, and keep each claim next to the record it came from. The ticket arrives with the history assembled and a recommendation: answer it, escalate it, or turn it into engineering work.

Every example on this page comes from our own support queue, with the customers anonymized. We run our support through a companion we call Fritz, and the skills below are the portable version of how it works.

blocks.text: Bring Strawberry the customer work already in front of you: the ticket you have been avoiding, the account that looks quiet, the customer who signed yesterday. Your companion picks the smallest useful piece of it and shows you the result before anything is sent or changed.

skill.context: Here's the ticket I've been avoiding. Tell me what happened before I reply.

sections.title: See the full story behind a ticket

blocks.text: Back to the customer whose credits never arrived. Strawberry checked the payment processor, the credit grant, the usage ledger, the live balance, and the app's own event log. The payment had gone through. The credits landed about two seconds later. The complaint came roughly six minutes after that, with no usage in between. The money was right and the balance was right. The window the customer was looking at was showing a stale counter.

That changes the reply completely. Nobody needs to issue a refund or grant the credits a second time. The customer needs to relaunch the app and see their current balance, and engineering needs to know that a counter can go stale after a top-up. A look at the ticket alone would have produced a kind, fast, wrong answer.

The same habit matters for accounts, not only tickets. One of our customer champions looked inactive: chat usage flat, credit usage flat, the usual cue to send a worried check-in. Strawberry widened the check to browser and integration activity first. In about three and a half minutes it found more than 1,500 background actions across five connected tools, including 172 calendar calls during the three quiet days. The champion had stopped typing and let the product run. The second seat on the account had almost no activity of any kind, and that was the person who needed onboarding.

items.title: Check whether a quiet account is really quiet
items.text: Usage across chat, browser, and integrations, plus the goals and promises on record, so one flat metric does not send the wrong email to the wrong person.

skill.context: Review the customer's progress, current signals, evidence gaps, and next actions.

items.title: Walk into the renewal knowing what was promised
items.text: Twenty minutes before a check-in, QBR, or renewal call, you need the few things that could derail it: unmet commitments and who made them, usage that dropped, the open ticket nobody mentioned.

skill.context: Prepare for a customer conversation using the account context that could change it.

items.title: Leave the call with a name next to every next step
items.text: Notes that split into customer follow-up on one side and internal actions with an owner on the other.

skill.context: Preserve the decisions, commitments, and follow-through from a customer conversation.

sections.title: Draft the reply from the records

blocks.text: The reply Strawberry drafted for the missing-credits customer did not open with an apology for a problem that had not happened. It confirmed the payment and the credit grant, with times, explained that the balance on screen was out of date, gave the relaunch steps, and said what engineering was now looking at. Short and specific, because every line had been checked against a record before it was written.

The opposite mistake is just as easy. A customer wrote in frustrated that they were paying but being treated as a free user. The account they wrote from was on the free plan and had hit its limit, so a shallow check would have told them they were wrong. Strawberry compared the customer's other logins, found the paid subscription sitting on a different one, corrected the internal diagnosis, and emailed them which login held the plan. About twelve minutes from complaint to answer.
Point Strawberry at the whole queue and it does the same reconstruction for each case, using your team's own priority and escalation rules rather than a severity score it invented.

items.title: Triage the queue by what is at stake
items.text: Priority, next action, and a first response for each ticket, using your team's rules. Forty overnight tickets become the three to read before standup.

skill.context: Triage this customer request using the team's actual rules and current context.

items.title: Investigate before you answer
items.text: The full thread, the account's history, current docs, known issues, and what your team's policy says, reconciled into a reply you can send.

skill.context: Find the strongest available answer and prepare a response for this customer and channel.

blocks.text: Engineering should never receive a link to a mystery ticket. One customer told us the app had stopped opening after an update. They had tried seven times over several days. On its own, that is a low-priority issue called "app won't launch" that waits in a backlog for a week.
Here is what Strawberry did with it, in under thirty minutes:

items: Joined the support report to release timing, product telemetry, error monitoring, and the relevant source code.
Isolated the failure to a point before the app's first window is even created.
Widened the search to everyone on the same version.
Found more than 80 previously active users matching a strict likely-regression definition.
Handed engineering a root-cause analysis and a minimal patch proposal.

blocks.text: One "it won't open" became an incident packet with a cohort attached, and engineering did not have to decide whether to care. The missing-credits case got the same treatment: a timestamped sequence, the failed-charge and missing-grant explanations already ruled out, and one question left for engineering to answer.

Once you approve the route and the boundaries, Strawberry recognizes when a case needs another team and prepares that handoff on its own. Customer-identifying detail stays in support. Engineering gets what engineering needs.

items.title: Send a human the full case
items.text: Impact, timeline, what has been tried, the customer's current message, and the specific decision the receiving team now owns.

skill.context: Prepare the customer-impact brief, current communication, exact internal ask, and next owner.

items.title: Create Jira or Linear issues from support tickets
items.text: Reproduce the problem, check for duplicates, and file an engineering issue that does not leak private customer context.

skill.context: Research and report the product bug while keeping customer-specific context appropriately scoped.

items.title: Keep it visible until it is resolved
items.text: The next update owed, the decision still open, and confirmation that the fix landed, tracked across support and the specialist team.

skill.context: Track the owners and unresolved commitments behind a customer escalation.

sections.title: Get a new customer to a first result

blocks.text: New customers did not buy a product tour. They bought whatever they need to get done this week. During one pilot, a new RevOps user gave Strawberry a task that was half research and half operations: go through a set of competitor websites, work out which customers were featured on them, and explain how to log those companies properly in their own systems. A messy Tuesday-morning job, not a tutorial.
Strawberry returned one output: the research, plus the operational next step written for that team's setup. The customer's reaction in the call notes was about as unambiguous as feedback gets.

That is what onboarding should feel like: the customer's own work, done well, early. Strawberry builds the onboarding path from the signed scope, the sales handoff, the stakeholders, and the setup dependencies, pointed at the outcome the customer named rather than a feature checklist.

items.context: Turn agreed goals and commitments into an owned path to first value.

sections.title: Turn resolved tickets into help docs

blocks.text: A recruiting team sent one thread with four complaints in it: a licensing change they believed had happened, search failures getting worse, agents getting stuck, and credits going missing. The tempting move is to find one cause and explain everything with it. Strawberry refused to assume the four shared a cause.

It confirmed the team's subscription was active and unchanged, so no licensing change had happened. It traced the missing credits to genuine use: almost the entire balance, across hundreds of individual actions. It read the screenshots and the results file the customer had attached, sent a targeted workaround for the search problem, and logged the stuck-agent behavior as a product signal for the team that owns it.
Then came the part that makes the next ticket faster. The licensing answer had taken investigation to confirm, so it became support documentation. The next person who asks gets it in a minute.

items.title: Publish the answer once
items.text: Turn a confirmed resolution or recurring question into help content the next customer can find, without duplicating an article that already exists.

skill.context: Turn verified current behavior into clear, findable customer documentation.

items.title: Show Product the pattern
items.text: Group feedback into themes, tensions, and examples with the original tickets still linked. A summary that informs the roadmap rather than pretending to be it.

skill.context: Turn customer feedback into themes, tensions, examples, and gaps with clear links to the sources.

blocks.text: Run one ticket from this week's queue through. It will get things wrong: too formal, escalated to the wrong team, citing a doc you retired months ago. Fix those and run another. After a handful, the corrections stop, and what is left is your team's support method, written down for the first time. Save it so the new hire handles a billing ticket the way your most experienced person does. Then put it on a schedule.

items.title: Set up the connected support system
items.text: Map the stack, learn from resolved cases, test the focused skills, and add Routines only after the manual flow works.

skill.context: Use Strawberry's published support method as a starting point, then adapt it to the systems and decisions your team already trusts.

items.title: Share the method with the team
items.text: Keep a trusted workflow as a team skill so colleagues follow the same checks, boundaries, and handoffs.

skill.context: Turn a trusted customer workflow into a shared team method with clear context, ownership, review points, and stop conditions.

blocks.text: A Routine repeats the check. It never grants permission to send, refund, change an account, file an issue, or publish. That stays with a person, and it matters more than it sounds.

One customer had been trying to cancel for nearly a month. Earlier automated replies kept telling them the request was with the team. No handoff had happened and no cancellation had happened, only the language of action. Strawberry reconciled the conversation against the live subscription and the latest payment, carried out the approved cancellation and refund, re-read the final account state, and confirmed the result in the customer's original channel, about 25 minutes from start to finish. Saying something was done and doing it are different actions, and Strawberry checks the second before it claims the first.
